title: Modeling the Impact of Integrating HIV and Outpatient Health Services on Patient Waiting Times in an Urban Health Clinic in Zambia
abstract: BACKGROUND: Rapid scale up of HIV treatment programs in sub-Saharan Africa has refueled the long-standing health policy debate regarding the merits and drawbacks of vertical and integrated system. Recent pilots of integrating outpatient and HIV services have shown an improvement in some patient outcomes but deterioration in waiting times, which can lead to worse health outcomes in the long run. METHODS: A pilot intervention involving integration of outpatient and HIV services in an urban primary care facility in Lusaka, Zambia was studied. Data on waiting time of patients during two seven-day periods before and six months after the integration were collected using a time and motion study. Statistical tests were conducted to investigate whether the two observation periods differed in operational details such as staffing, patient arrival rates, mix of patients etc. A discrete event simulation model was constructed to facilitate a fair comparison of waiting times before and after integration. The simulation model was also used to develop alternative configurations of integration and to estimate the resulting waiting times. RESULTS: Comparison of raw data showed that waiting times increased by 32% and 36% after integration for OPD and ART patients respectively (p<0.01). Using simulation modeling, we found that a large portion of this increase could be explained by changes in operational conditions before and after integration such as reduced staff availability (p<0.01) and longer breaks between consecutive patients (p<0.05). Controlling for these differences, integration of services, per se, would have resulted in a significant decrease in waiting times for OPD and a moderate decrease for HIV services. CONCLUSIONS: Integrating health services has the potential of reducing waiting times due to more efficient use of resources. However, one needs to ensure that other operational factors such as staff availability are not adversely affected due to integration.

summary.oneLiner: Integrating HIV and outpatient services in a Lusaka clinic raised waiting times, but simulation suggests operational changes, not integration itself, explain much of the rise.
summary.overview: Zambian clinics that merged HIV treatment with general outpatient care saw patients wait longer, which can discourage care. The authors timed patients for one week before and one week after integration at one urban clinic, then used a computer simulation of the clinic to separate the effect of integration from other changes such as lower staff availability and longer breaks between patients. They report that much of the raw increase was explained by these other operational changes, and that integration itself may have reduced waiting times if no extra steps were added. Adding staff for the new steps could bring waits back to pre-integration levels, according to their model.
summary.question: How much of the rise in patient waiting times after integrating HIV (ART) and outpatient (OPD) services is caused by integration itself, and how much by other operational changes, and which integration configurations reduce waiting times?
summary.method: Time and motion study of patient flow, with t-tests comparing periods, followed by discrete event simulation (ARENA software) of the clinic before and after integration, run for 200 replications. The simulation was used to control for differences in staffing, patient mix and breaks, and to test alternative configurations such as adding staff, partial integration and different ART-to-OPD patient ratios.
summary.data: One urban primary care clinic in Lusaka, Zambia. Two seven-day observation periods: June 23-29, 2008 (before integration) and January 19-25, 2009 (about six months after). Observations covered the busiest clinic hours, 7:30 am to 12:00 noon. The daily patient load was approximately 80 (50 OPD and 30 ART patients).
findings: Raw data showed waiting times increased by 32% for OPD patients and 36% for ART patients after integration (p<0.01).

Simulation suggests a large portion of the increase could be explained by changes in operational conditions, such as reduced staff availability (p<0.01) and longer breaks between consecutive patients (p<0.05).

Controlling for these differences, integration per se would have resulted in a significant decrease in waiting times for OPD and a moderate decrease for HIV services, according to the abstract; the simulation's version of integration without added steps was associated with lower waits.
Adding PITC and registration/vitals steps for OPD patients increased waiting times in the simulation, even with added staff.
Including four healthcare workers for registration and PITC (one more than current practice) would bring waiting times at or below pre-integration levels for ART and OPD patients in the model.
Integrating only the clinical officer or only the pharmacy step gave waiting times not substantially higher than full integration, according to the model.
Higher ART patient shares were associated with lower waiting times overall, and higher PITC uptake was associated with longer OPD waits but shorter ART waits.
The authors caution that the single-clinic, short-observation design limits generalisation, and that the findings should not be taken at face value.
summary.whyItMatters: The authors argue that rising waits should not be attributed to integration without deeper analysis, and that managers should protect staff availability and plan for added steps (such as PITC) with extra staff. They suggest partial integration may be a feasible option where full cross-training is not possible, and that district managers could use patient mix and PITC uptake to choose clinics for integration. They also note that simulation with post-integration data can help policymakers anticipate effects before implementation.
